kernels.definition: A list is an ordered collection of values written in square brackets; each element has an index, beginning at 0.

definitionAnchor.quote: A list object can be used to bundle elements together in Python

facts.text: A list is written with square brackets [] holding comma-separated values.

anchor.quote: A list is defined by using square brackets [] with comma separated values within the square brackets

facts.text: Individual elements are accessed directly using an index.

anchor.quote: Individual list elements can be accessed directly using an index

facts.text: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.

anchor.quote: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence

facts.text: A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order.

anchor.quote: An iterative for loop can be used to iterate through a list

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §3.4 List basics; §9.1 Modifying and iterating lists

kernels.definition: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.

definitionAnchor.quote: A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs

facts.text: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.

anchor.quote: a dictionary object cannot hold duplicate key values

facts.text: Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §10.1 Dictionary basics

kernels.definition: A string is a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0; slicing extracts a contiguous substring with the [a:b] notation.

definitionAnchor.quote: A string is made up of a sequence of characters indexed from left to right, starting at 0

facts.text: For a string s, the left-most character is index 0 and the right-most is index len(s) - 1.

anchor.quote: the left-most character is indexed 0 and the right-most character is indexed len(s) - 1

facts.text: Negative indexing refers to characters from right to left starting at -1.

anchor.quote: Negative indexing can also be used to refer to characters from right to left starting at -1

facts.text: A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive).

anchor.quote: starting from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive) is returned

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.4 String basics; §8.2 String slicing

kernels.definition: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.

definitionAnchor.quote: Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function

facts.text: open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.

anchor.quote: Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function

facts.text: read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.

anchor.quote: The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string

facts.text: readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.

anchor.quote: The readlines() function reads the individual lines of a file and returns a string list containing all the lines of the file in order

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §14.1 Reading from files

kernels.definition: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem; a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.

definitionAnchor.quote: Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem

facts.text: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input.

anchor.quote: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input

facts.text: The process continues until the problem is small enough that the solution is known or easily found — the base case.

anchor.quote: The recursion process continues until the problem is small enough, at which point the solution is known or can easily be found

facts.text: Without a base case that stops the self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.

anchor.quote: without it the calls would never stop

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §12.1 Recursion basics

kernels.definition: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.

definitionAnchor.quote: In a Python program, a class defines a type of object with attributes (fields) and methods (procedures)

facts.text: A class is a blueprint for creating objects.

anchor.quote: A class is a blueprint for creating objects

facts.text: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.

anchor.quote: Individual objects created of the class type are called instances

facts.text: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

anchor.quote: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

mcItems.q: A student has the list [10, 20, 30]. Which access returns the middle value directly?
op: numbers[0]
numbers[1]
numbers[2]
numbers[3]
mcItems.ex: numbers[1] is correct because list indexes start at 0, so the middle value is at index 1. A common misconception is to count the first element as 1 and choose numbers[2], but that would select the last value here.

mcItems.q: What does a for loop do when it runs through a list of names?
op: It visits each element in order
It changes every element automatically
It starts at the last element first
It uses only the final element
mcItems.ex: It visits each element in order is correct. A plausible misconception is that a loop would jump to the last item or mutate items by itself, but the listed behavior is only iteration through the elements in sequence.

keyTerms.df: A position number used to access one element in a sequence.
keyTerms.eg: In ["a", "b", "c"], the element "b" is at index 1.
keyTerms.mi: It begins at 1 because lists are usually counted from one.
keyTerms.cx: Indexes for these lists begin at 0, so the first element is at index 0.

keyTerms.df: The punctuation used to write a list and hold its values.
keyTerms.eg: [3, 5, 7] is a list written with square brackets.
keyTerms.mi: They are only for indexing, not for writing the list itself.
keyTerms.cx: The same brackets are used to write the list form directly.

mcItems.q: A student stores a grade in a mapping under the key "Maya". Later, which access pattern matches how the structure works?
op: Look up the grade by the key "Maya".
Look up the grade by its position number.
Store two separate grades under the same key "Maya".
Use braces only after ordering the entries.
mcItems.ex: A dictionary retrieves a value by its key, so the grade is found with "Maya". A position-based lookup is the plausible misconception, but that fits an ordered numeric container rather than a key-value mapping.

mcItems.q: A lab note needs labels like "title", "author", and "year". Which choice best matches the structure described?
op: A curly-brace mapping from labels to values.
A numbered list that depends on order.
A mapping that allows the same label twice.
A text block that cannot be labeled.
mcItems.ex: A dictionary is written in curly braces with key: value form and fits naturally labeled data. The tempting alternative is an ordered list, but that uses position rather than labeled lookup and does not match the key-based design.

keyTerms.df: A key-value mapping that retrieves each value by its key, not by position.
keyTerms.eg: A course roster could map "Maya" to her saved grade.
keyTerms.mi: It works like a numbered list, so you find items by position.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that lookup uses the label key, while position-based access is the misleading alternative.

keyTerms.df: A repeated label that a key-based mapping cannot hold as a second entry.
keyTerms.eg: Trying to store two values under the key "year" in one mapping.
keyTerms.mi: Two identical labels can both stay in the same mapping as separate pairs.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the same key cannot be duplicated because the value is found through that key.

mcItems.q: In the string s = "boundary", which result comes from s[2:5]?
op: "und"
"oun"
"boun"
"ndar"
mcItems.ex: The correct slice starts at index 2 and stops before index 5, so it returns characters 2, 3, and 4. A common misconception is to treat the end index as included; if that were true, "ound" would fit, but slicing excludes the character at b.

mcItems.q: For the string t = "python", what character does t[-1] select?
mcItems.ex: Negative indexing counts from the right starting at -1, so t[-1] is the right-most character, "n". A plausible mistake is to think -1 means the first character or an out-of-range error, but for strings it names the last position.

keyTerms.df: A contiguous part of a sequence taken with bracket notation and two bounds.
keyTerms.eg: In lab work, s[2:5] pulls a middle piece of a file name or token list.
keyTerms.mi: It includes the item at the stop bound.
keyTerms.cx: The stop bound is excluded, so the last returned character is at b - 1.

keyTerms.df: Position counting that starts from the right side instead of the left.
keyTerms.eg: In the string "python", index -1 points to "n".
keyTerms.mi: It means the string is traversed backward for every access.
keyTerms.cx: Only the index numbering changes; the string itself is not reversed.

mcItems.q: A student opens a file and wants all of its contents as one text value. Which function best matches that goal?
op: open()
read()
readline()
readlines()
mcItems.ex: read() is the best match because it returns the entire contents as a single string. A plausible mistake is choosing readline(), but that method returns only the next single line rather than the whole file.

mcItems.q: A program is already working with an open file object and needs a list containing every line. Which method should it use?
op: read()
open()
readlines()
readline()
mcItems.ex: readlines() fits because it returns a list with every line of the file. A common misconception is to use read(), but that produces one string for the full file instead of a list of lines.

keyTerms.df: A program uses a file by opening it, reading from or writing to it, and then closing it.
keyTerms.eg: A script opens a text file, reads its contents, and later writes updated results into another file.
keyTerms.mi: It only means sending data into a file.
keyTerms.cx: The source describes both directions: programs can read information from files and write information into files, so one-way writing is incomplete.

keyTerms.df: A file method that produces a list containing each line from the file.
keyTerms.eg: A grader loads a log file and stores all lines so each entry can be handled separately.
keyTerms.mi: It returns one single string with the whole file.
keyTerms.cx: That behavior belongs to read(); readlines() returns a list of lines, which keeps line boundaries instead of merging everything into one string.

mcItems.q: A student writes a function that processes a list by calling the same function on the remaining items until nothing is left. Which choice best matches that design?
op: It solves a larger task by dividing it into unrelated tasks
It calls itself on a smaller input until a base case ends the process
It repeats the same input forever without a stopping point
It changes the problem into a different problem with a new algorithm
mcItems.ex: Correct: it uses self-calls on a smaller input and stops at a base case. A common misconception is to think recursion must switch to a different algorithm; in fact, the same problem is handled in simpler form rather than replaced by a new method.

mcItems.q: A recursive routine keeps calling itself, but there is no smallest case where the answer is already known. What is the most likely outcome?
op: It finishes early because the first call is always enough
It stops after one self-call and returns a fixed result
It never terminates and overflows the call stack
It becomes iterative once the input gets smaller
mcItems.ex: Correct: without a base case, the self-calls do not stop, so the calls continue until the stack overflows. A plausible but source-inconsistent idea is that shrinking the input alone is sufficient; shrinking helps, but termination still depends on a base case.

keyTerms.df: The stopping condition that makes the answer known or easy to find.
keyTerms.eg: A recursive list function returns immediately when the list is empty.
keyTerms.mi: It is the step that makes the problem larger.
keyTerms.cx: The recursive calls handle smaller inputs; the base case ends the chain.

keyTerms.df: A reduced version of the same task used for the next self-call.
keyTerms.eg: A function recurses on the rest of a list rather than the whole list again.
keyTerms.mi: It means the code must change to a different problem.
keyTerms.cx: The task stays the same in kind; only the input becomes smaller each time.

mcItems.q: A student has the list [10, 20, 30]. Which access returns the middle value directly?
op: numbers[0]
numbers[1]
numbers[2]
numbers[3]
mcItems.ex: numbers[1] is correct because list indexes start at 0, so the middle value is at index 1. A common misconception is to count the first element as 1 and choose numbers[2], but that would select the last value here.

mcItems.q: What does a for loop do when it runs through a list of names?
op: It visits each element in order
It changes every element automatically
It starts at the last element first
It uses only the final element
mcItems.ex: It visits each element in order is correct. A plausible misconception is that a loop would jump to the last item or mutate items by itself, but the listed behavior is only iteration through the elements in sequence.

mcItems.q: A student stores a grade in a mapping under the key "Maya". Later, which access pattern matches how the structure works?
op: Look up the grade by the key "Maya".
Look up the grade by its position number.
Store two separate grades under the same key "Maya".
Use braces only after ordering the entries.
mcItems.ex: A dictionary retrieves a value by its key, so the grade is found with "Maya". A position-based lookup is the plausible misconception, but that fits an ordered numeric container rather than a key-value mapping.

mcItems.q: A lab note needs labels like "title", "author", and "year". Which choice best matches the structure described?
op: A curly-brace mapping from labels to values.
A numbered list that depends on order.
A mapping that allows the same label twice.
A text block that cannot be labeled.
mcItems.ex: A dictionary is written in curly braces with key: value form and fits naturally labeled data. The tempting alternative is an ordered list, but that uses position rather than labeled lookup and does not match the key-based design.

keyTerms.df: A key-value mapping that retrieves each value by its key, not by position.
keyTerms.eg: A course roster could map "Maya" to her saved grade.
keyTerms.mi: It works like a numbered list, so you find items by position.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that lookup uses the label key, while position-based access is the misleading alternative.

keyTerms.df: A repeated label that a key-based mapping cannot hold as a second entry.
keyTerms.eg: Trying to store two values under the key "year" in one mapping.
keyTerms.mi: Two identical labels can both stay in the same mapping as separate pairs.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the same key cannot be duplicated because the value is found through that key.

mcItems.q: In the string s = "boundary", which result comes from s[2:5]?

"boun"
"ndar"

mcItems.q: For the string t = "python", what character does t[-1] select?
mcItems.ex: Negative indexing counts from the right starting at -1, so t[-1] is the right-most character, "n". A plausible mistake is to think -1 means the first character or an out-of-range error, but for strings it names the last position.

keyTerms.cx: The stop bound is excluded, so the last returned character is at b - 1.

keyTerms.cx: Only the index numbering changes; the string itself is not reversed.
